L189: 
L190: Location(s): cite51†​Dawson Creek L191: 
L192: Welders weld ferrous and non-ferrous metals in all positions, on both plate and pipe, using SMAW (Shielded Metal Arc Welding), GTAW (Gas Tungsten Arc Welding), and FCAW (Flux-Cored Arc Welding) processes.
L193: Welders use manual or semi-automatic welding equipment. They use flame-cutting, brazing, and air-arcing equipment. Additionally, they use brakes, shears, and other metal straightening and bending machines. They generally plan work from drawings or by analyzing the job tasks, determine the materials required and welding processes, then use their knowledge to complete the job. Welders use blueprint symbols to determine machining operations.
L194: They check product specifications using precision measuring instruments, maintain equipment and replace parts when required. Welders use a logbook to record training, competencies, certifications, endorsements and employment history.
L195: Welders may specialize in certain types of welding, such as custom fabrication, shipbuilding and repair, pressure vessel welding, pipeline construction welding, structural construction welding or machinery and equipment repair welding.
L196: Students who complete the Welder Foundation program will receive Levels 1 and 2 technical training and 300 work-based hours credit toward completing their Welder Apprenticeship. Certified welders will qualify to test for Pressure Welding IT Procedure tests administered by Technical Safety BC (TSBC).

L198: There is a reading week in this program typically at the end of February.

L204: ## Career Prospects
L205: Welders can specialize in certain types of welding such as custom fabrication, shipbuilding and repair, pressure vessel welding, pipeline construction welding, structural construction welding or machinery and equipment repair welding. Welders can find employment with companies that manufacture structural steel and plate work, boilers, heavy machinery, aircraft, ships, and other metal products, and by welding contractors and welding shops. They also may be self-employed in the industry.

L253: 
L254: Complete either A, B, or C:

L256: ### A. English and Math
L257: #### English Requirement
L258: One of the following:
L259:   * BC Language Arts 10 Courses – 4 credits earned, minimum individual grade of C+, or equivalent.
L260:   * BC Language Arts 11 Courses – 4 credits earned, minimum individual grade of C+, or equivalent.
L261:   * BC Language Arts 12 Courses – 4 credits earned, minimum individual grade of C+, or equivalent.
L262:   * cite89†ENGL 030 or higher, with a minimum final grade of C+, or equivalent.
L263:   * IELTS score of 5.5 overall with no band less than 5.0 or equivalent English placement test and score.
L264: #### Math Requirement

L266: 
L267:   * BC Math 10 with a minimum final grade of C+, or equivalent
L268:   * BC Math 11 with a minimum final grade of C, or equivalent
L269:   * BC Math 12 with a minimum final grade of C, or equivalent
L270:   * cite90†MATH 030 or higher, with a minimum final grade of C+, or equivalent.

L284: ## Important Notes
L285:   1. The program is eligible for Canada Student Loans. Visit cite93†Student Aid BC†studentaidbc.ca to apply for financial assistance online.  Note that dual credit students are not eligible for Student Aid.
L286:   2. Students must provide personal protective equipment (CSA approved leather boot with safety toe and shank, clear lense safety glasses, flame resistant coveralls, welders’ safety clothing, leather gloves, leather jacket or apron, welding helmet, and cutting goggles).  Students are required to have a computer (laptop or other mobile device) with cite94†minimum computer requirements .
L287:   3. The program is affiliated with cite95†SkilledTradesBC†skilledtradesbc.ca , SD 59, 60, 81 and 87.

L76: ## Overview
L77: 
L78: In this electrical foundation program you’ll gain essential Level 1 technical training. Learn theory and skills from workplace safety to blueprint reading and wiring methods for residential and light commercial construction.
L79: 
L80: This program offers an eight-week foundational module that covers important basics such as technical vocabulary, workplace safety standards and industry engagement.

L177: ## Your path to Red Seal Certification
L178: 
L179: Foundation Apprenticeship Getting started Supports
L180: ### Foundation
L181: 
L182: NIC’s trades cite9†foundation programs equip you with the basic knowledge and skills needed to enter a trade without requiring an employer sponsor.
L183: 
L184: Upon completion of a foundation program, you’ll receive Level 1 technical training and some work-based training hours when you register as an apprentice.
L185: 
L186: Completing a foundation program can make it easier to find employment and sponsorship to continue as an apprentice, since you’re entering the trade with some experience.
L187: ### Apprenticeship
L188: 
L189: Most apprenticeships take four or more years to complete, with 80% of the training at the worksite under the supervision of a certified tradesperson and 20% in-class technical training.
L190: 
L191: You can choose to seek employer sponsorship for an apprenticeship right away or you can complete a foundation program for Level 1 training first.
L192: ### Getting started
L193: 
L194: cite59†Find your trade†skilledtradesbc.ca and become familiar with how many levels of training you need, the number of work-based hours required and information about your exams.
L195: 
L196: ### Supports
L197: 
L198: During your technical training, you are eligible to apply for financial supports with WorkBC Employment Services and Service Canada. Visit SkilledTradesBC for more info.
L199: 
L200: cite60†Learn more†skilledtradesbc.ca L201: 
L202: ## Frequently asked questions
L203: ## [Button: What are the differences of levels for trades training, like Harmonized or Apprenticeship? ]
L204: 
L205: Typically, NIC offers:
L206: 
L207:   * Pre-apprenticeship (Foundation) programs: Level 1 Foundation training to prepare for entry-level positions.
L208:   * Apprenticeship programs: A combination of on-the-job training and classroom instruction, Level 1-4.
L209:   * Specialized certifications: Training in specific skills or safety standards, such as welding or forklift operation.
L210: ## [Button: How do I become an apprentice? ]
L211: 
L212: Visit cite61†SkilledTradesBC†skilledtradesbc.ca to learn how to become an apprentice.
L213: 
L214: ## [Button: Is trades training suitable for women and underrepresented groups? ]
L215: 
L216: Absolutely! Colleges and industries actively encourage diversity in trades.
L217: ## [Button: Can I work while studying trades? ]
L218: 
L219: International students are allowed to work off campus up to 24 hours per week. You can work unlimited hours off campus during scheduled NIC breaks (e.g. reading week, winter holidays).
L220: 
L221: ## [Button: Who can I contact for more information? ]
L222: 
L223: Contact study@nic.bc.ca for guidance on the program, requirements and application procedures.
